section_summary: This section consists of Peruvian newspaper clippings from August–September 1937 concerning the alleged “Japanese infiltration” of Peru, especially Japanese participation in cotton farming, landholding, commerce, industry, and immigration. The clippings combine supportive letters, economic and legal arguments for restrictions, accounts of Japanese activity in Huaral and Chancay, and broader discussions of Japanese trade and migration in Latin America and Brazil. They also include Japanese journalist H. Ikeyama’s rebuttal and Guillermo Salinas Cossío’s response, followed by an explicitly racist and eugenicist argument for European immigration and the exclusion of Asians.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa — letter from Manuel Romero La Puente
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping of an open letter
subfiles.about: A correspondent endorses La Prensa’s campaign and argues that Japanese state support enables Japanese immigrants to dominate Peruvian cotton farming and related commerce.
subfiles.summary: Romero La Puente claims Japanese cotton farming reflects organized government policy, with an integrated network of credit, transport and shops forming a Japanese state within Peru, and calls for legislation.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa — letter from Chancay
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping of an anonymous letter
subfiles.about: An anonymous Chancay resident alleges that Japanese interests control nearly all of the valley’s agricultural estates.
subfiles.summary: Anonymous Chancay letter: most estates are under a Japanese concern or Japanese tenants, only Huando is wholly Peruvian, and control of land means control of the economy.

subfiles.title: Expansión Comercial Japonesa, I
subfiles.about: An economic essay explains the rapid expansion of Japanese foreign trade through state organization, currency depreciation, and low labor costs.
subfiles.summary: Article with Japanese trade statistics for 1927-1936 crediting export cartels, state direction, devaluation and low wages, urging Peruvians to copy Japanese discipline while defending national interests.

subfiles.title: Apreciaciones de la Sociedad Pro-Marina sobre un importante problema
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping of an institutional letter
subfiles.from: Asociación Nacional Pro-Marina, represented by J. E. de Mora and Isaías Combe
subfiles.about: Pro-Marina praises the newspaper’s campaign and warns that Japanese agricultural and commercial practices threaten Peruvian economic independence and sovereignty.
subfiles.summary: Sociedad Pro-Marina endorses Salinas Cossio's arguments on Japanese acquisition of agriculture, contrasting exclusionary Japanese businesses with other immigrants, and calls for immediate limits.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa — “Voz de aliento” and “Otra voz”
subfiles.from: Asociación Nacional Pro-Marina; Carlos Moreyra y P. S.
subfiles.about: Two communications support the campaign against Japanese agricultural expansion and discuss legal controls on immigration, foreign labor, and land tenancy.
subfiles.summary: Pro-Marina and Carlos Moreyra attribute Japanese cotton gains to government backing and low living standards and review Law No. 7505 and 1936-1937 decrees on quotas and a foreigners' census.

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa — commerce and industry
subfiles.about: An editorial broadens the newspaper’s campaign from agricultural landholding to Japanese retail, food-service, beverage, and manufacturing activity.
subfiles.summary: Editorial portrays Japanese commerce as a coordinated system, focusing on cafes, chicha, soft-drink plans and workshops' employment quotas, and approves restrictions on Japanese cotton textiles.

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa — letter from Jorge Muñante Gómez
subfiles.about: A correspondent supports strict control of organized Japanese economic activity while disclaiming hostility toward Japanese people as such.
subfiles.summary: Munante Gomez praises La Prensa and Salinas Cossio for warning of Japanese absorption of agriculture and industry, framing regulation as economic nationalism.

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa — history of Japanese occupational expansion
subfiles.about: An editorial traces Japanese immigrants’ purported movement from agricultural labor into urban trades, retailing, industry, transport, education, and landownership.
subfiles.summary: Editorial history: Peru recruited Japanese laborers after Japan beat Russia; they left plantations, accumulated capital in trades, then built businesses and returned to farming as a cohesive, expansionist colony.

subfiles.title: La ocupación japonesa de los valles de Huaral y Chancay
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping of a signed article or letter
subfiles.about: A correspondent alleges extensive Japanese control over agriculture, commerce, services, and institutions in Huaral and Chancay.
subfiles.summary: Gonzalez claims Japanese tenants displaced Peruvians and held about ninety percent of Huaral's cultivated area, and invokes Law No. 7505 to defend local peasants.

subfiles.title: El Japón y el comercio, II
subfiles.about: A long essay connects Japanese commercial expansion with state-directed industry, imperial strategy, nationalist ideology, and competition in Asia and Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Salinas ascribes Japan's export growth to demography and a national mission attributed to Matsuoka and Hata, viewing commerce and expansion as one imperial system, with competition and cotton efforts in Latin America.

subfiles.title: La inmigración en el Brasil y el problema japonés
subfiles.about: An essay reviews Brazil’s population distribution, immigration history, racial composition, and legislative response to rising Japanese immigration.
subfiles.summary: Hauser reviews Brazil's low population density, the rapid rise of Japanese arrivals as the largest contingent in 1934, and the constitutional two-percent quota affecting them.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa — letter from H. Ikeyama and “Un punto sobre cada i”
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping of a covering letter and rebuttal article
subfiles.to: Director and readers of La Prensa
subfiles.about: The director of Perú Jiho requests space to rebut Salinas Cossío’s account of Japanese trade and to correct his sources and factual claims.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama accuses Salinas of anti-Japanese bias resting on Upton Close, alleging a fabricated Close interview, and corrects claims about Matsuoka's mother and Sugimura.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa — Salinas Cossío’s reply to H. Ikeyama
subfiles.to: H. Ikeyama and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: Salinas denies that his campaign is driven by anti-Japanese prejudice and defends his focus on Japanese acquisition of Peruvian cotton land.
subfiles.summary: Salinas replies that Ikeyama ignored his economic arguments, denies relying only on Close or hostility to Japanese people, and accepts minor corrections.

subfiles.title: El mejoramiento de la raza y la inmigración asiática
subfiles.about: An explicitly racist and eugenicist essay advocates European and Anglo-American immigration while urging restrictions or prohibition on Asian immigration.
subfiles.summary: Opinion piece tying national reconstruction under Benavides to racial homogeneity, preferring European immigration and calling Asians inferior, and urging enforcement of the Porras-Kulinfang treaty.
